findings.headline: Time-weighted average credit score of 1.90 against 4.34 for the six NI council average, per Arlingclose benchmarking.

findings.matters: Counterparty risk and return on cash are compared across peer councils, so a finance director elsewhere would use this benchmark to assess their own investment approach.
findings.figures: Average credit score 1.90 against 4.34 for the six NI council average; investment return 3.96% against 3.98%; 9 counterparties or funds against 8 on average

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 Prudential and Treasury Management Indicators
findings.headline: Cash available within three months of £34m at 30.09.26 against a 2026/27 target of £10m.
findings.detail: The paper reports liquidity against a voluntary measure of cash available for unexpected payments within a rolling three-month period without additional borrowing. Cash and cash equivalents were £46.6m at 30.09.26, up from £46.4m at 30.06.26.
findings.matters: Cash held against a set liquidity target shows how much headroom the council has before needing to borrow, which lenders and peer finance teams both look at.
findings.figures: Cash available within 3 months £34m at 30.09.26 against target £10m; cash and cash equivalents £46.6m at 30.09.26, £46.4m at 30.06.26; loans £27.3m at 30.09.26

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 Prudential and Treasury Management Indicators
findings.headline: Council says loans for completed projects will be drawn over a shorter period than originally intended.
findings.detail: The paper says the council has several completed projects for which borrowing is still to be drawn. It states these loans will be drawn over a shorter period than originally intended, saving some loan interest.
findings.matters: A council drawing borrowing faster than planned, to cut interest, is a change to its borrowing profile that a finance director elsewhere could compare with their own plans.
findings.quote: These loans will be drawn over a shorter period

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 Prudential and Treasury Management Indicators
findings.headline: 10-year annuity loan rate of 6.05% at 30.09.26, up from 5.33% at 30.06.26.
findings.detail: The paper tabulates annuity loan rates across five terms at four dates. The 10-year rate moved from 5.33% at 30.06.26 to 6.05% at 30.09.26, with the 40-year rate at 6.87%.
findings.matters: The cost of new borrowing is what the council will pay to replace cash or fund its forecast borrowing requirement, and a finance director at another council would compare it with their own quotes.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 Prudential and Treasury Management Indicators
findings.headline: Liability benchmark forecast rising from £3.9m at 31.3.27 to £79.8m at 31.3.29.
findings.detail: The paper says the council currently holds surplus cash, but based on current projections a borrowing requirement is expected to arise in the medium term. The liability benchmark table shows the forecast rising sharply across the three years.
findings.matters: A council moving from surplus cash to a borrowing requirement will need to raise new funding, which is a direct signal to lenders and to finance directors comparing their own forecasts.
findings.figures: Liability benchmark £3.9m (31.3.27 forecast), £28.4m (31.3.28 forecast), £79.8m (31.3.29 forecast); existing borrowing £28.4m (31.3.27), £26.3m (31.3.28), £24.2m (31.3.29)
findings.quote: However, based on current projections, a borrowing requirement is expected to arise in the medium term.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 Prudential and Treasury Management Indicators
findings.headline: Council has not borrowed for several years, using surplus cash instead; loans of £27.3m at 30.09.26 against a Capital Financing Requirement of £45.6m.
findings.detail: The paper says the council has used surplus cash, generated from surpluses and in-year capital savings, in place of borrowing for capital projects. It also says several completed projects still have borrowing to be drawn.
findings.matters: A council funding capital from cash rather than new loans is a position a finance director elsewhere could compare against, and a lender would want to know when that borrowing will be drawn.
findings.figures: Loans £27.3m at 30.09.26; Capital Financing Requirement £45.6m at 30.09.26; Capital Financing Requirement £44.7m at 31 March 2026
findings.quote: Council have not borrowed for several years and have instead made use of surplus cash

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 Prudential and Treasury Management Indicators
findings.headline: Strabane Public Realm and DNA Museum spend to 30.09.26 of £530k and £1,883k, against £4.5m and £9.3m originally estimated for 2026/27.
findings.detail: The paper lists half-year spend of £530k on Strabane Public Realm and £1,883k on the DNA Museum. It says both projects were originally estimated to incur significant spend in 2026/27, and that a significant portion of spend may move into 2027/28.
findings.matters: Large projects moving into the next financial year change the timing of borrowing and cash needs, which matters to both the council's finance team and anyone funding it.
findings.figures: Strabane Public Realm £530k spent to 30.09.26 against £4.5m originally estimated for 2026/27; DNA Museum £1,883k spent to 30.09.26 against £9.3m originally estimated for 2026/27
findings.quote: Projects originally estimated to incur significant spend in 2026/27 included Strabane Public Realm (£4.5m)

findings.detail: The paper reports capital spend of £7.4m in the first half of the year against a full-year estimate of £38.7m. It says an updated 2026/27 capital profile will be reported with the 2027/28 estimates.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council, or a lender, would compare half-year capital spend with the annual estimate to judge whether the programme is on track.
findings.figures: £38.7m estimated 2026/27 capital expenditure; £7.4m spent April to September 2026
findings.quote: Capital Expenditure £38.7m £7.4m

findings.matters: The split of airport subvention between central government and council funding is a cost-sharing arrangement other councils with airports or similar grant-funded services can compare.

findings.detail: The paper says the council's district rates element is around 57% of this total. It also says £1.575m has been built into rating forecasts for old debt write-off, and that there is a significant risk of further write-off in the current rating year.
findings.matters: Non-collection of rates debt is a risk to income that finance directors and lenders assess when reviewing a council's collection performance.
findings.figures: £11.7m total debt from previous rating years; £5.97m red status; circa 57% council share; £1.575m built into forecasts for old debt write-off
findings.quote: there is £11.7m of total debt in the rating system for this Council area relating to previous rating years of which £5.97m has been allocated red status by LPS.

findings.headline: The council's District Fund reserve is planned to fall from £750k in 2026/27 to £500k in 2027/28, with a 0.3% rates impact.
findings.detail: The reserve is being used to fund recurrent service expenditure. The paper says Members may consider whether 2026/27 surpluses can reduce the rates impact, and this will be reviewed at Quarter 3.
findings.matters: A planned step-down in a recurrent reserve draw is the kind of commitment finance directors compare when assessing reserve sustainability.
findings.figures: £750k drawn in 2026/27; £500k in 2027/28; 0.3% rates impact
findings.quote: The agreed reserves reduction strategy requires this to reduce to £500k in 2027/28 with an associated 0.3% rates impact.

findings.headline: Leisure income is well ahead of budget at Quarter 2 at the Tier 1 sites, by £708k, though the income budget has not been increased.
findings.detail: The paper says leisure income budgets have not been increased for 2026/27 usage because of ongoing business case work for new strategic leisure facilities. Cost pressures in utilities (£130k) and maintenance offset part of the gain.
findings.matters: Income growth not yet built into budgets is relevant to how other councils treat strategic leisure business cases and forecasts.
findings.figures: £708k leisure income ahead of budget at Q2 (Tier 1 sites); utility overspend £130k; other costs overspend £114k
findings.quote: Leisure Income continues to be well ahead of budget in Q2 (£708k) for the Tier 1 Sites

findings.headline: Savings target of £160k was achieved at Quarter 2, with a £67k surplus reported, subject to using the £530k Special Projects budget.
findings.detail: The paper says the savings target was set as part of rates finalisation. The surplus depends on applying the £530k Special Projects budget to the waste contracts overspend.
findings.matters: Reaching a savings target at mid-year is a point other finance officers can compare, and the caveat shows the surplus depends on a one-off budget.
findings.figures: £160k savings target; £80k at Quarter 2; £67k surplus; £530k Special Projects budget
findings.quote: Achieved for Quarter 2 given that small positive £67k surplus position reported although subject ito utilisation of special projects budget of £530k

findings.headline: The council says it will continue to use capital savings to revenue-finance completed capital projects, to minimise borrowing.
findings.detail: The paper describes this as a central element of the agreed capital funding strategy, using loan charges set aside for projects not yet complete. The £711m programme of investment is cited as the context.
findings.matters: A council that uses capital savings to fund completed projects in place of borrowing is reducing its external borrowing need, which is relevant to lenders and to peers with similar strategies.
findings.figures: £711m ongoing programme of investment; Major projects budget £12,390,975 annual
findings.quote: where possible to revenue finance completed capital projects and minimise the need to borrow/ save on loan interest.

findings.headline: £950k of investment surplus has been transferred to the capital fund at Quarter 2 to reduce future borrowing for strategic leisure projects.
findings.detail: The transfer is made after ensuring the revised reserves reduction strategy can be achieved, under a Members' agreement that investment surpluses from capital fund monies go to the capital fund.
findings.matters: A transfer that reduces future borrowing for strategic leisure projects changes the council's expected borrowing requirement, which is relevant to a lender.
findings.figures: £950k transferred at Quarter 2; total transfers to reserves £1.385m including £120k leisure VAT and £210k leisure income surplus
findings.quote: £950k has therefore been transferred in this regard at Quarter 2.

findings.headline: Investment interest of £962k was received in the first six months, which the paper describes as well ahead of budget.
findings.detail: The paper attributes this to significant sums on long-term deposit, mainly from capital savings linked to strategic leisure projects, and to current high interest rates. Members have agreed that surplus investment income is transferred to the capital fund to reduce future borrowing.
findings.matters: Holding capital savings on deposit to offset future borrowing is a treasury approach that other councils and lenders can compare against their own borrowing plans.
findings.figures: £962k investment interest received in six months; well ahead of budget
findings.quote: Investment interest of £962k received during the 6 mths from money market funds, secured deposits and other

findings.headline: £530k of the £1.6m unallocated Special Projects budget is proposed to cover the waste contracts overspend, with the figure expected to rise to £1.1m by year end.
findings.detail: The paper states that the £530k proposal is at Quarter 2 and that the paper notes it will likely rise to £1.1m. It also says this will be a significant recurrent consideration for the 2027/28 rates estimates.
findings.matters: Using one-off unallocated funds for a recurring cost is a pressure other councils also face, and the paper flags it as a rates-setting issue.
findings.figures: £1.6m unallocated; £530k proposed at Quarter 2; expected to rise to £1.1m by year end
findings.quote: it is proposed that £530k of this is used to address the waste contracts overspend at Quarter 2

findings.headline: The Environment directorate shows a Quarter 2 variance of (£516,649), with waste contracts being over budget by £530k.
findings.detail: The paper attributes the overspend to waste volumes (£330k) and fuel surcharges (£200k), partly offset by a rates refund for the Skeoge depot (£138k). The waste and fuel overspends are earmarked in the Financial Contingency Reserve but have not yet been applied at Quarter 2.
findings.matters: Waste contract costs are an overspend that is expected to grow into the next financial year, which will feed into the 2027/28 rates estimates.
findings.figures: (£516,649) revised variance; waste contracts £530k over budget; increased volumes £330k; fuel surcharges £200k; vehicle fuel costs £197k; rates refund £138k
findings.quote: being over budget (£530k) as a result of increased volumes (£330k)

findings.headline: The rates support grant has not been reinstated to its previous £20m+ level, the paper says, despite council submissions and a judicial review process.
findings.detail: The paper says the council has made numerous submissions to the Departmental grant review and taken part in the Mid Ulster judicial review. It also records that the council has been advised of a 23.46% share of the regional pot, which it has assumed stays at £3.124m, and describes this as a significant risk.
findings.matters: Reduced central grant shifts more of the cost of council services onto local ratepayers, which is a funding pressure other councils in Northern Ireland face on the same grant review.
findings.figures: 23.46% regional pot share; £3.124m assumed regional pot (2025/26 level); previous grant level £20m+
findings.quote: no significant progress has been achieved towards reinstatement of the grant to it's previous (£20m+)

findings.headline: 275 concluded 2023 Revaluation challenges have removed £4.095m of rateable value from the council's non-domestic list.
findings.detail: The paper states this is a 24.9% value reduction on the properties appealed and about £1.69m of lost recurrent rates income. A further 89 cases remain, with £5.758m gross value, which the council estimates could lose a further £590k if concluded in the same proportion.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council facing 2023 appeals can compare the 24.9% reduction and the per-case loss against their own exposure.
findings.figures: 275 concluded challenges; £4.095m rateable value removed; 24.9% value reduction; circa £1.69m recurrent rates lost; 89 remaining cases; £5.758m gross value; £590k potential further loss
findings.quote: To date, 275 concluded challenges against the 2023 Revaluation list have resulted in £4.095m of rateable value being removed from Council's non domestic list.

findings.headline: LPS forecasts a £605k positive rates finalisation figure for 2026/27 at Quarter 2, which the council has not yet reported as a variance.
findings.detail: The paper attributes £91k to domestic growth and £504k to non-domestic growth including derating grant. The council has retained a £1.9m provision in its Financial Contingency reserve rather than reporting the £605k.
findings.matters: Rates are the council's largest income source, and the paper shows a forecast gain being held back against appeal and debt-write-off risk.
findings.figures: £605k forecast positive rates finalisation; £91k domestic; £504k non-domestic; £1.9m provision (£350k recurrent)
findings.quote: LPS are forecasting a positive rates finalisation figure of £605k at the end of Quarter 2.

findings.detail: The paper links the higher CPI rate, up from 2.6% in June 2026, to a likely rates impact from pay awards and other pressures. It also lists waste contract pressures, 1.5% capital investment and possible grant cuts.
findings.matters: A finance director would compare the stated rates impact of pay awards against the inflation trend, which determines how much rates pressure other councils face in their own 2027/28 processes.
findings.figures: circa 2%-2.5% rates impact; CPI 3.5% in September 2026; 2.6% in June; 1.5% rates investment
findings.quote: could likely result in a circa 2%-2.5% rates impact for pay awards alone

findings.detail: The paper says the council's Rates Support Grant allocations for 2026/27 are unconfirmed and that the regional pot could be reduced because of Executive budgetary pressures. It describes this as a significant risk.
findings.matters: Government grant allocations that remain unconfirmed mid-year are a funding risk that councils across Northern Ireland share, and the council says it has been unable to reinstate the grant to earlier levels.
findings.figures: 23.46% share; £3.124m regional pot; RSG £730k in the budget
findings.quote: It has been assumed that the regional pot will be retained at its 2025/26 level of £3.124m

findings.headline: Leisure facilities produced a £709k saving, which the council has ringfenced for its strategic leisure projects.
findings.detail: The paper says the leisure saving is net of leisure cost pressures and is ringfenced towards the strategic leisure projects. Other income surpluses include Building Control (£74k), Business grants (£140k), Culture (£115k) and cemeteries (£26k).
findings.matters: A savings source being directed to a capital programme rather than service budgets is an approach other councils funding leisure projects would compare with their own.
findings.figures: £709k leisure facilities saving; £120k leisure VAT savings and £210k leisure surplus transferred to reserves
findings.quote: The key saving relates to leisure facilities (£709k)

findings.headline: The £80k Quarter 2 milestone of a £160k 2026/27 savings target is reported as achieved, against an overall surplus position.
findings.detail: The paper says the £80k up to Quarter 2 must be reported as a pressure against budgets, but it is counted as achieved because of the overall surplus.
findings.matters: Savings targets that are met on the back of a surplus rather than from specific savings may not be repeated, which a finance officer elsewhere would want to see.
findings.figures: £160k full-year savings target; £80k up to Quarter 2 target
findings.quote: Whilst the £80k up to Quarter 2 target must be reported as a pressure against budgets, it has been achieved given the overall small surplus position reported.

findings.detail: The Capital Financing Requirement is £45.6m, against an authorised limit of £49m. The paper says the council is keeping investment income, leisure surpluses and loan charge savings in reserve to reduce the borrowing required.
findings.matters: A lender would track a council's borrowing trajectory against its authorised limit, and the paper signals a significant increase once the leisure projects start.
findings.figures: £27.3m borrowing at 30/9/26; £29.1m at 31/3/26; £45.6m Capital Financing Requirement; £49m authorised limit; £140m strategic leisure projects
findings.quote: Borrowing levels are expected to increase significantly once

findings.detail: The paper says the surplus comes from money market funds, secured deposits and other councils, and reflects large sums on long-term deposit from strategic leisure project capital savings. It also states that investment income for the six months was £962k, against £1.714m for the year ended 31/3/26.
findings.matters: Investment income funded by capital savings for future borrowing shows how a council is trying to reduce the borrowing it will need for its leisure projects.

findings.quote: an investment income surplus of £950k has been reported for the period

findings.headline: Council holds £4.69m in its Financial Contingency Reserve for risks that emerged after the 2026/27 rates process.
findings.detail: The paper says the reserve covers possible Government grant cuts, non-domestic appeals and bad debt write-off, and provision for waste and utility volatility. The paper also says £435k of service surpluses has been transferred to reserves and ringfenced for leisure and other projects.
findings.matters: A finance director would want to know the size of the contingency reserve and what it is being held against, since the council is choosing to protect it rather than release the rates surplus.
findings.figures: £4.69m Financial Contingency Reserve; £435k transferred from services to reserves
findings.quote: Council retains a sum of £4.69m within its financial contingency reserve

findings.headline: Council plans to draw £750k from its District Fund in 2026/27 to fund recurrent service expenditure, reducing to £500k in 2027/28.
findings.detail: The paper says the reserves reduction strategy carries an associated 0.3% rates impact in 2027/28. It reports a £375k overspend in grants and reserves, which relates to this drawdown.
findings.matters: Using reserves to fund recurrent spending, with a planned step-down, is a funding choice that other councils with similar strategies will recognise, and it carries a rates consequence.
findings.figures: £750k drawdown in 2026/27; £500k in 2027/28; 0.3% rates impact; £375k grants/reserves overspend
findings.quote: Council plans to utilise £750k from its District Fund during 2026/27 to fund recurrent service expenditure.

findings.detail: The paper says £1.575m has been built into forecasts for old debt write-off. It notes that after significant write-off in 2025/26, there is a risk of further write-off in the current rating year.
findings.matters: Rating debt write-off erodes income, and a lender or finance director would want the size of the legacy debt and the share that falls to district rates.
findings.figures: £11.7m total rating debt from previous years; £5.97m red status; circa 57% district rates share; £1.575m built into forecasts
findings.quote: there is £11.7m of total debt in the rating system for this Council area relating to previous rating years

findings.headline: 275 concluded non-domestic rating challenges have removed £4.095m of rateable value, with 89 challenges still open on a £5.758m gross value.
findings.detail: The paper says the concluded challenges represent a 24.9% reduction in the appealed properties and a loss of about £1.69m in recurrent rates income. If the remaining cases are settled in a similar proportion, it estimates a further £590k loss, with backdated rebates.
findings.matters: Revaluation appeals on the 2023 list are a rates income risk for councils across Northern Ireland, and the paper quantifies both the settled and outstanding exposure.
findings.figures: 275 concluded challenges; £4.095m rateable value removed; 24.9% reduction; circa £1.69m lost recurrent income; 89 open cases with £5.758m gross value; further £590k loss estimated
findings.quote: To date, 275 concluded challenges against the 2023 Revaluation list have resulted in £4.095m of rateable value being removed from Council's non domestic list.

findings.headline: Land and Property Services forecasts a £605k positive rates finalisation at Quarter 2, which the council has not reported as a variance.
findings.detail: The forecast consists of £91k from domestic growth and £504k from non-domestic growth, including derating grant. The paper says the council has not reported this at this early stage and retains a £1.9m provision in its Financial Contingency Reserve.
findings.matters: A finance officer at another council would note that a favourable rates forecast is being held back as a provision rather than booked, because of appeals and debt write-off risk.
findings.figures: £605k positive finalisation forecast; £91k domestic; £504k non-domestic; £1.9m provision retained (£350k recurrent)
findings.quote: Surprisingly, LPS are forecasting a positive rates finalisation figure of £605k at the end of Quarter 2.

findings.headline: Utility costs are £361k over budget, with £130k from leisure facilities and £197k from fleet fuel.
findings.detail: The paper attributes the utility overspend to electricity, gas, oil and vehicle fuel, citing ongoing global volatility.
findings.matters: Energy and fuel cost overspends are a common pressure across councils, and the paper shows how they are split between leisure and fleet.
findings.figures: £361k over budget; £130k leisure facilities; £197k fleet fuel
findings.quote: which are over budget by £361k due to ongoing global volatility

findings.headline: Waste contracts are £530k over budget, made up of £330k from higher waste volumes and £200k from fuel surcharges.
findings.detail: The paper identifies waste contracts as the key pressure facing the council. It says this will be a significant recurrent consideration for the 2027/28 rates estimates.
findings.matters: A recurring cost of this size, driven by volumes and fuel surcharges, will feed into the next rates setting, and other councils with housing growth and waste contracts face the same pressures.

findings.quote: The key pressure facing Council is waste contracts which are over budget by £530k.

findings.detail: The paper says the outturn is £57k ahead of target, but this depends on using £530k from the Special projects budget, which is derived from the PEPR levy. It also states that services are £17k overspent overall, with other costs showing a £450k surplus.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council would see that a reported in-year surplus rests on a one-off transfer from a special projects budget, and that the underlying service position is an overspend.

findings.quote: Members will note that the outturn is currently £57k ahead of target at Month 6.

findings.detail: The Strategic Programme Director updated members on the City Deal portfolio, which the paper says shows continued progress and challenges. Priorities named were the delivery challenges for the School of Medicine and Digital Innovation Hub, strategic public realm projects, and enabling infrastructure including transport, car parking and NI Water infrastructure. The paper does not give cost, programme or funding figures for any of these.
findings.matters: Named City Deal capital schemes with delivery problems and dependent enabling infrastructure are the kind of slippage a finance director at a partner council would want to track against its own capital programme.
findings.quote: addressing delivery challenges around the School of Medicine and Digital Innovation Hub

findings.paper_title: Appendix A Com Dev funding DfC Budget Interim Allocations Q3
findings.headline: The Department for Communities faces continued significant uncertainty regarding its final budget settlement from the Executive
findings.detail: The Department states it continues to 'operate within a highly challenging financial environment' and notes that 'While discussions on the Executive's Budget continue, there remains significant uncertainty regarding the Department's final Resource DEL allocation.' The Department indicates it 'must retain sufficient flexibility to manage within its eventual Budget settlement once agreed.'
findings.matters: The cascading budget uncertainty across the Executive and Department signals systemic constraints in the council's public finance environment and reduces the council's ability to plan multi-year service delivery based on normal partnerships.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: While discussions on the Executive's Budget continue, there remains significant uncertainty regarding the Department's final Resource DEL allocation.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A Com Dev funding DfC Budget Interim Allocations Q3
findings.headline: Sector organizations are directed to curtail spending and avoid new commitments pending final budget settlement
findings.detail: The Department instructs funded organizations to 'manage expenditure prudently, curtail spending where possible and avoid entering into new commitments unless essential.' The letter warns that the interim allocation 'should not be interpreted as an indication of, or commitment to, the level of funding available for the remainder of 2026-27.'
findings.matters: If the council depends on these organizations to deliver services or programs, the planned reduction in their activity will reduce service capacity and may shift demand onto the council or leave service gaps unmet.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: organisations should continue to manage expenditure prudently, curtail spending where possible and avoid entering into new commitments unless essential.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A Com Dev funding DfC Budget Interim Allocations Q3
findings.headline: Voluntary and community sector organizations are receiving funding only through 31 December 2026 pending completion of the Executive's Budget process
findings.detail: The Department for Communities has issued only a three-month interim allocation (1 October to 31 December 2026) to sector organizations while awaiting confirmation of its own budget allocation from the Executive. The Department confirms 'there remains no confirmed Departmental Resource DEL allocation against which final funding decisions can be made' and 'there remains significant uncertainty regarding the Department's final Resource DEL allocation.'
findings.matters: Organizations that deliver or support council services face cash-flow uncertainty beyond December; the council should anticipate possible service delivery gaps from January 2027 onwards and may need to plan alternative provision.
findings.figures: Interim allocation period: 1 October 2026 to 31 December 2026; payments commence week commencing 5 October 2026
findings.quote: To maintain business continuity, I am issuing a further interim allocation covering the period 1 October 2026 to 31 December 2026, pending agreement of a final Budget and subsequent allocation decisions.

findings.headline: Treasury Reserve treatment uncertainty creates additional downside risk to allocation
findings.detail: The Department identifies the treatment of the 2025-26 Treasury Reserve Claim as a specific uncertainty that could trigger further reductions to the Department's overall allocation, and thereby to councils' settlements.
findings.matters: This is a named, specific risk that could compress the council's budget further beyond the baseline, requiring contingency planning on top of existing constraints.

findings.headline: Flat cash position with no funding allocated for pay and inflationary pressures

findings.headline: Capital projects face delivery delays that could push spend and borrowing into future years
findings.detail: The council notes that capital projects including Strabane Public Realm (£4.5m), Riverine green infrastructure (£9.5m) and the DNA Museum (£9.3m) face uncertainty in delivery timelines. Q1 actual capital spend was only £3.7m against an annual estimate of £38.7m, indicating programme is still ramping. The council explicitly states that significant project spend may slip from 2026/27 into 2027/28 due to funding availability and contract timelines.
findings.matters: Project delays affect both the timing and accuracy of financial forecasts. If major capital programmes slip years, this could accelerate or defer the borrowing requirement and impact the council's debt trajectory.
findings.figures: Q1 spend £3.7m of £38.7m annual estimate (9.6%); delayed projects worth £27.8m identified
findings.quote: As with all capital programmes, there is a degree of uncertainty around the deliverability of these projects in line with the original plans, particularly due to factors such as funding availability and contract timelines. While some expenditure has already been, and will continue to be, incurred in 2026/27, a significant portion of spend on these projects may into the 2027/28 year.

findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement forecast to more than double from £44.7m to £99.2m by 2029
findings.detail: The council's CFR is forecast to increase sharply over three years, rising from the current actual of £44.7m to £99.2m by March 2029. This reflects the council's substantial capital investment plans and indicates the scale of assets being funded through borrowing or reserves. The growth accelerates from 2027/28 onwards (£57.8m) suggesting capital programmes front-loaded into that year.
findings.matters: CFR growth indicates the council's capital ambitions and the level of financing required. Lenders need to understand whether this capital growth is deliverable and how it will be financed given the reserve depletion forecast.
findings.figures: CFR progression: 44.7 (March 2026 actual) → 43.8 (2027 forecast) → 57.8 (2028 forecast) → 99.2 (2029 forecast)

findings.headline: Council forecast to shift from cash surplus to substantial borrowing requirement by 2028/29
findings.detail: The liability benchmark shows the council currently holds surplus cash but is forecast to require £18.4m borrowing in 2028 and £69.8m by 2029. This represents a significant transition from the council's current position, where it has not borrowed for several years and has instead used surplus cash to fund capital projects. The forecast reflects declining balance sheet resources (reserves declining from £59.9m to £29.4m over three years) and rising capital needs.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the trajectory of the council's liquidity and borrowing need. The forecast shift to substantial borrowing (£70m+) against current borrowing of £28.4m represents a material change in financial profile and debt servicing requirements.
findings.figures: Forecast borrowing requirement 2029: £69.8m; Current borrowing: £28.4m; Balance sheet resources declining from £59.9m (2026) to £29.4m (2029)
findings.quote: However, based on current projections, a borrowing requirement is expected to arise in the medium term.

findings.headline: Repayment of interest-free City Deal loan extended to 30 June 2026
findings.detail: The interest-free loan from the Department for Communities issued in 2023/24 for Strabane Academy Lands purchase was originally due for repayment on 31 March 2026 but has been extended to 30 June 2026. This extension was not sought for rate management but necessary for cash management.
findings.matters: An extension of a government interest-free loan suggests the council could not repay from operational resources at the originally scheduled date, indicating cash constraints at year-end.
findings.figures: Loan amount not stated in this extract
findings.quote: The repayment date for the interest-free loan, issued by the Department for Communities in 2023/24 in relation to the purchase of Strabane Academy Lands under the City Deal, has been revised from 31 March 2026 to 30 June 2026.

findings.headline: Council is systematically funding capital from revenue to avoid borrowing, reducing planned debt by £14.4m
findings.detail: Rather than borrowing to fund capital projects as originally planned, the council has used direct revenue contributions and minimum revenue provision to fund capital, eliminating £14.4m of planned borrowings. This strategy has saved approximately £8.9m of interest over the life of assets.
findings.matters: This represents a deliberate choice to prioritize debt reduction over revenue flexibility. While it reduces interest costs, it means less cash available for services and leaves the council more reliant on grants/receipts to fund future capital.
findings.figures: £14.4m of loans avoided, £8.9m interest saving
findings.quote: Council has continued to finance some projects previously earmarked to be funded by borrowings in 2025/26 by both direct revenue contributions and minimum revenue provision charges. Since the implementation of this strategy, approximately £14.4m of loans will no longer need to be drawn saving circa £8.9m of loan interest

findings.headline: Capital expenditure came in 38% below revised budget with no explanation
findings.detail: Original capital forecast was £30.3m, revised down to £28.1m in February 2026, but actual outturn was only £17.4m. The document lists specific projects totalling £17.2m but provides no explanation for why delivery fell so far short of the revised estimate made just one month before year-end.
findings.matters: Unexplained capital underspend suggests either delivery constraints (land, planning, procurement delays) or reluctance to commit capital, either of which could affect future capital plans and borrowing requirement timing.
findings.figures: Original £30.3m, revised £28.1m, actual £17.4m
findings.quote: In February 2026, the revised anticipated level of capital expenditure for 2025/26 was £28.1m. The actual level of capital expenditure in 2025/26 was £17.4m

findings.headline: Rating system shows £12.97m debt with £6.41m in red status and £4.13m in amber, plus recent large write-offs
findings.detail: The rating debt system carries £12.97m arrears (57% relating to District rates), with £6.41m classified as red status (highest risk) and £4.13m as amber. The council notes significant debt write-offs occurred in 2025/26 and identifies ongoing risk of increased write-off requirements.
findings.matters: Large write-off provisions and high-status debt indicate collection risk materialising; successive years of write-offs suggest structural collection problems.
findings.figures: £12.97m total rating debt; £6.41m red status; £4.13m amber status; £1.575m provision for old debt write-off
findings.quote: there is £12.97m of total debt in the rating system for this Council area relating to previous rating years of which £6.41m has been allocated red status by LPS and a further £4.13m has been allocated amber status.

findings.headline: Council drawing down £750k from reserves in 2026/27 to fund recurrent service expenditure
findings.detail: The council plans to use £750k of its District Fund reserves to fund recurrent spending in 2026/27. The reserves reduction strategy requires this to fall to £500k in 2027/28, with an associated 0.3% rates impact.
findings.matters: Using reserves to fund recurrent spending is unsustainable; the trajectory shows reserves are being depleted to close a structural funding gap.
findings.figures: £750k drawdown planned 2026/27; reducing to £500k in 2027/28; 0.3% rates impact associated
findings.quote: Council plans to utilise £750k from it's District Fund during 2026/27 to fund recurrent service expenditure. The agreed reserves reduction strategy requires this to reduce to £500k in 2027/28 with an associated 0.3% rates impact.

findings.headline: Rates support grant held at 2025/26 reduced level (£3.124m) with risk of further cuts if Executive budgets cut
findings.detail: The council's grant assumption of £3.124m remains unchanged from 2025/26 but is flagged as a significant risk given that Executive budgets are not yet confirmed and clear central budgetary pressures exist. The council notes this is down from previous levels of £20m+.
findings.matters: Rates grant is a key income stream; the unexplained £17m+ reduction from historical levels and the explicit risk flag suggest further cuts are possible mid-year.
findings.figures: Assumed 2025/26 level of £3.124m; historical level was £20m+
findings.quote: the regional pot will be retained at it's 2025/26 level of £3.124m, however, this remains a significant risk given that Executive budgets have not yet been confirmed and clear central budgetary pressures exist.

findings.headline: 106 live non-domestic rate revaluation appeals could result in £500k further loss of recurrent income
findings.detail: 192 revaluation appeals concluded in Q1 reduced properties by over 21% and cost the council £800k in lost income. If the remaining 106 live cases settle at a similar rate, the council projects a further £500k loss of recurrent rates income.
findings.matters: Rates are the council's single most critical income source; this appeal pipeline represents material unquantified risk to recurrent funding.
findings.figures: 106 live appeals; 192 concluded at 21%+ reduction; potential £500k additional loss; £5.943m NAV at risk
findings.quote: If the remaining properties were to be concluded successfully in a similar proportion, this would result in a further loss of recurrent rates income to Council of £500k with associated rebates backdated accordingly.

findings.headline: Waste contracts £270k over budget in Q1 due to volume increases and fuel surcharges
findings.detail: The Environment service is facing waste contract costs of £270k above budget, split between £125k from increased waste volumes and £145k from fuel surcharges. The council notes this may be offset by using unallocated Special Projects funding (£1.6m remains available) if necessary.
findings.matters: Waste cost inflation is recurring and unplanned; projecting this Q1 overspend annualises to £1.08m, potentially constraining finances or requiring reserve use.
findings.figures: £270k overspend (£125k volumes, £145k fuel surcharges)
findings.quote: waste contracts being over budget (£270k) due to increased volumes (£125k) and fuel surcharges (£145k)

findings.headline: District Fund reserve drawdown strategy commences, reducing from £750k draw to £500k in 2027/28
findings.detail: Council is drawing £750k from its District Fund to finance recurrent service expenditure in 2026/27, planned to reduce to £500k in 2027/28 with a 0.3% rates impact. This indicates reliance on reserve depletion rather than full rate recovery for ongoing operations.
findings.matters: Signals structural funding gap and reserves erosion; limits financial flexibility for future shocks
findings.figures: £750k drawdown 2026/27; £500k drawdown 2027/28; 0.3% rates impact for reduction
findings.quote: Council plans to utilise £750k from its District Fund during 2026/27 to fund recurrent service expenditure. The agreed reserves reduction strategy requires this to reduce to £500k in 2027/28 with an associated 0.3% rates impact.

findings.detail: As of Q1 reporting, staff pay awards for 2026/27 remain outstanding with a full and final 3.3% offer not yet accepted. findings.quote: Pay awards have not yet been confirmed for 2026/27. A full and final 3.3% offer has not been accepted at this point

findings.headline: £140m strategic leisure projects programme will drive significant increase in borrowing once construction commences
findings.detail: Current borrowing stands at £28.4m; council expects this to increase materially once the £140m leisure projects (strategic projects and City Deal) move to construction. Interim strategy involves ringfencing investment income, leisure surpluses and capital loan charge savings to minimise borrowing requirement, but this is acknowledged as a key component of capital funding strategy.
findings.matters: Major long-term debt commitment that will reshape council's financial profile and debt service obligations
findings.figures: £140m leisure projects; current borrowing £28.4m; Capital Financing Requirement £45.2m; capital expenditure budget £13.932m annually
findings.quote: Borrowing levels are expected to increase significantly once Council's £140m strategic leisure projects progress to construction and, it is therefore important to ensure that all investment income returns, leisure income surpluses and capital loan charges savings in the interim are ringfenced where possible to reduce this requirement.

findings.detail: Council's budget assumes 23.46% share of a £3.124m regional pot (2025/26 level), but this remains at risk because Executive budgets have not been confirmed and clear central budgetary pressures exist. Funds have been retained in the contingency reserve against this risk. This continues a long history of underfunding for the council.

findings.figures: £3.124m assumed (23.46% share); £730k RSG in approved budget

findings.detail: Total waste collection and disposal cost £14.338m in 2025/26, £500k over budget driven by increased volumes and fuel surcharges. Council has retained £600k contingency for ongoing waste contract volatility in reserves, indicating officers expect these pressures to persist.
findings.matters: Cost pressures in a major service budget signal either unplanned demand growth or exposure to uncontrolled commodity/fuel costs, either of which could require future budget adjustments if they persist.

findings.detail: Council is executing a multi-year capital strategy, particularly for strategic leisure facilities at Templemore and Strabane alongside community projects. In 2025/26, £13.882m was transferred from capital budget (£7.874m), leisure budgets (£1.827m), and investment income (£1.081m) to cover commitments. This strategy is designed to minimise future borrowing by using operating surpluses.
findings.matters: Large capital commitments create future servicing costs and borrowing obligations. If project costs overrun or revenues underperform, the council may need to either increase borrowing or draw further on reserves at a time when reserves are already declining.
findings.figures: £711m ongoing programme; £13.882m transferred to reserves in 2025/26 (£7.874m capital, £1.827m leisure, £1.081m investment income); funded by 1.5% rates investment

findings.detail: Council is executing a planned reserves reduction strategy, drawing down District Fund from £7.015m (8.57% of budget) to £5.815m (5.97%) over four years. The £243k surplus this year was partly achieved by avoiding the planned £900k draw-down. By 2027/28, additional 0.3% rates investment will be needed; this same challenge repeats through 2028/29 and 2029/30.
findings.matters: Declining reserve buffers reduce financial flexibility for unexpected pressures. The target 5–7.5% guidance means the council will be at the minimum threshold, with limited capacity to absorb additional income shocks from rates appeals or grant cuts.
findings.quote: This current projection requires a 0.3% rates investment as part of the 2027/28 rates process and beyond which will be a challenge.

findings.headline: Non-domestic revaluation appeals have permanently eroded £3.5m of annual rates income, with 108 live appeals presenting further downside risk
findings.detail: Since 2023, 575 revaluation appeals concluded with average 22.5% value reduction, causing £3.5m permanent loss to recurrent income (4.4% of rates). A further 108 live appeals with £7.72m NAV could cost another £600k if similar outcomes occur, plus backdated rebates potentially exceeding £1.8m. This is described as Council's most critical funding source.
findings.matters: Rates are the council's primary income stream (£80m of £82m budget). Structural erosion from appeals directly threatens revenue sustainability and forces reliance on reserves or rates rises.
findings.figures: £3.5m recurrent loss from 575 concluded appeals; 108 live appeals with £7.72m NAV; potential additional loss £600k + rebates >£1.8m; £2.0m contingency provision retained

findings.detail: The council states 'external funding opportunities have become significantly more challenging in recent times due to Government budgetary constraints.' findings.quote: Whilst Council will continue to explore all possible external funding opportunities, the external funding environment has become much more challenging and it is clear that Council's strategy of 1.5% rates investment into it's capital programme will be required beyond 2027/28 to ensure continued progress across remaining priorities.

findings.committee: Special Meeting of Derry City and Strabane District Council
findings.headline: PWLB interest rate sensitivity directly affects project affordability by up to £7m
findings.detail: At 6% interest over 40 years, the council can borrow £139m. At 6.50%, only £132m. Current PWLB rates on 23 January 2026 are 6.16%. The council is exploring the National Wealth Fund to save 0.4% but notes this facility is 'subject to criteria' which could mean 'part/all of the required borrowing may not be available from this source.'
findings.matters: A 75 basis point move in interest rates directly reduces available finance and directly threatens affordability of the leisure projects. This is a material live risk with limited mitigation options secured.
findings.figures: At 5.75% interest: £143m available; at 6%: £139m; at 6.50%: £132m (£11m range). Current rates 6.16%.
findings.quote: As an example, at the initial targeted 6% interest over 40 years, this would enable Council to borrow £119m plus cash reserves of £20m, leaving the total available for the projects at £139m. PWLB interest rates are linked to Government gilt rates which have been volatile due to economic and UK budget uncertainty.

findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement projected to more than double to £101.8m by 2028/29

This sharp increase reflects the strategic leisure projects and other capital commitments. The council remains in an under-borrowed position but this trajectory suggests increasing reliance on debt.
findings.matters: A doubling of the financing requirement signals a structural change in the council's balance sheet. It reflects growing capital intensity and suggests sustained high capital spending is now embedded in the council's plans.
findings.figures: CFR current year £47.2m, Year +3 (2028/29) £101.8m; Gross borrowing current £31.6m, Year +3 £99.7m

findings.committee: Special Meeting of Derry City and Strabane District Council
findings.headline: New leisure facilities face £465k annual revenue shortfall, potentially rising to £1m by 2030

findings.figures: Current shortfall £465k, forecast £1m by 2030 based on 3% inflation, represents 1.25% rates implication
findings.quote: Based on current costs and prices (i.e. if these facilities were to open in 2025/26), there would be a revenue shortfall of £465k. This figure will increase due to pay and cost inflation between now and the facilities being opened. As an estimate, based on 3% inflation, the revenue shortfall could equate to circa £1m by 2030- this would represent a further 1.25% rates implication.

findings.committee: Special Meeting of Derry City and Strabane District Council
findings.headline: Two major strategic leisure projects need £143.91m of council funding, with no funding fully secured
